notes.exam_tips_md:
- Draw band diagrams with the insulator gap clearly largest (diamond 5.5 eV, Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV); energy bands are qualitative only.
- Doped crystals are neutral; donors are pentavalent, acceptors trivalent; name the majority and minority carriers.
- In diode circuits decide forward or reverse bias first, then subtract 0.7 V (Si) or 0.3 V (Ge) only for a conducting diode.
- Rectifiers: circuit, waveforms and output frequency (f for half-wave, 2f for full-wave); ripple ΔV = It/C.
- LED forward, photodiode reverse, solar cell no bias; Zener reverse across the load with a series resistor, I = I_Z + I_L.

cards.front_md: Why do energy levels become bands in a crystal?
cards.back_md: Electrons of neighbouring atoms interact and no two may share a state, so each level splits into N close levels.

cards.front_md: Valence band, conduction band, forbidden gap?
cards.back_md: Outer electrons fill the valence band; the next band up is the conduction band; the empty energy range between them is the forbidden gap Eg.
The valence and conduction bands overlap (or the conduction band is part-filled): no gap.
Full valence band, empty conduction band, large gap (diamond 5.5 eV).

cards.front_md: Band gaps of Ge and Si?
cards.back_md: Ge about 0.7 eV; Si about 1.1 eV.

cards.front_md: Why does a semiconductor conduct more when warmed?
cards.back_md: More electrons cross the gap, making more electron–hole pairs; the resistance falls.

cards.front_md: Longest wavelength that crosses a gap Eg?
cards.back_md: λ = hc/Eg = 1240/Eg nm (Eg in eV). Silicon: 1127 nm.
Its 5.5 eV gap is bigger than any visible photon (1.8–3.1 eV), so none is absorbed.
A pure crystal; thermal energy makes equal numbers of free electrons and holes.
A vacant covalent bond that acts as a mobile carrier of charge +e; it drifts opposite to the electrons.
Adding a tiny amount (about 1 atom in 10⁷) of a suitable impurity to a pure semiconductor.
Pentavalent donor (P, As, Sb); electrons are the majority carriers, holes the minority.
Trivalent acceptor (B, Al, Ga, In); holes are the majority carriers, electrons the minority.
No: each free electron is balanced by a fixed positive donor ion.

cards.front_md: Where are donor and acceptor levels?
cards.back_md: Donor level just below the conduction band; acceptor level just above the valence band.
σ = e (nₑ μₑ + nₕ μₕ).
Diffusion and recombination of electrons and holes uncover fixed donor (+) and acceptor (−) ions with no mobile carriers.

cards.front_md: Barrier potential of Si and Ge?
cards.back_md: About 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium.
From the n side to the p side.
Battery + to p. Barrier falls to V₀ − V, region narrows, large current.
Battery + to n. Barrier rises to V₀ + V, region widens, tiny minority-carrier current.

cards.front_md: Why is the reverse current almost constant?
cards.back_md: It is carried by thermally generated minority carriers, whose number does not depend on the voltage.
rd = ΔV/ΔI on the forward characteristic.
Same as the input (50 Hz): one pulse per cycle.
Twice the input: 100 Hz on 50 Hz mains.
Gives two voltages equal and opposite in phase, so D₁ and D₂ conduct in turn.
Charges at the peaks and discharges slowly into the load, smoothing the pulses; ΔV ≈ It/C.
LED forward; photodiode reverse; solar cell no bias.
More of the input becomes light and less heat than in a filament lamp; they last longer; less fuel burnt, less pollution.
Zener reverse across the load with Rs in series; Vout = VZ; I = (Vin − VZ)/Rs; IL = VZ/RL; IZ = I − IL.

questions.stem_md: When N identical atoms are brought together to form a crystal, each sharp energy level of an isolated atom becomes a band of N closely spaced levels. This happens because

options.text_md: the nuclei of the atoms are displaced from their positions by the lattice vibrations
each atom gives up all its electrons to the other atoms of the crystal
the electrons of neighbouring atoms interact, and no two electrons may occupy the same state
the temperature of the crystal rises as the atoms come closer together

questions.solution_md: In the crystal the outer electrons of neighbouring atoms influence one another, and the exclusion principle does not allow N electrons to share one state, so each atomic level spreads into N slightly different levels that form a band — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Visible photons carry between about 1.8 eV (red) and 3.1 eV (violet). A pure crystal whose forbidden gap is 5.5 eV will therefore

options.text_md: be transparent and colourless, because no visible photon has enough energy to lift an electron across the gap
look black, because it absorbs every visible photon
conduct well at room temperature, because visible light excites its electrons
absorb only the violet end of the spectrum and look yellowish

questions.solution_md: Photon energy is $\dfrac{1240}{\lambda}$ eV: 700 nm gives 1.77 eV and 400 nm gives 3.10 eV, both below 5.5 eV. No visible photon can raise an electron from the full valence band to the empty conduction band, so the light passes through unabsorbed — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A germanium detector (forbidden gap 0.7 eV) is illuminated in turn by infrared lasers of wavelength 1064 nm, 1550 nm and 2000 nm, each of the same power. Using hc = 1240 eV nm, the radiation that can lift electrons across the gap is

options.text_md: 1064 nm and 1550 nm only
1064 nm only
all three wavelengths
1550 nm and 2000 nm only

questions.solution_md: Photon energy $\dfrac{1240}{\lambda}$: 1064 nm → 1.17 eV; 1550 nm → 0.800 eV; 2000 nm → 0.620 eV. A photon must carry at least 0.7 eV, so 1064 nm and 1550 nm work but 2000 nm (0.62 eV) does not — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A thin wafer of pure silicon is warmed from 300 K to 350 K. Its electrical resistance

options.text_md: rises, because the lattice vibrations scatter the carriers more, as in a metal
does not change, because the forbidden gap of silicon has a fixed value
falls, because more electrons are lifted across the gap and more electron–hole pairs are formed
rises, because electrons are removed from the conduction band by the heat

questions.solution_md: In a pure semiconductor heating creates many more free electrons and holes, and this increase of the number of carriers far outweighs the extra scattering by the lattice, so the resistance falls (a negative temperature coefficient) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Germanium has a larger forbidden gap than silicon, so it takes more energy to release an electron from a bond in germanium than in silicon.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The gap of germanium (about 0.7 eV) is smaller than that of silicon (about 1.1 eV), so less energy is needed to free an electron in germanium.

questions.stem_md: The band of energies lying between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band, in which a perfect crystal has no electron states, is called the forbidden ___.
questions.solution_md: The **forbidden gap** (energy gap, band gap) Eg.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Pure silicon is almost an insulator at very low temperatures, but it conducts slightly at room temperature.

**Reason (R):** At room temperature thermal energy lifts a few electrons from the valence band across the 1.1 eV gap into the conduction band.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: near 0 K the valence band is full and the conduction band empty, so there is no conduction; at room temperature a few thermally excited electrons (and the holes they leave) can carry a small current — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A silicon wafer (forbidden gap 1.1 eV) is lit by two beams, each of power 0.50 μW: one of wavelength 800 nm and one of wavelength 1300 nm. Assuming that every photon able to do so creates one electron–hole pair, find the number of pairs created per second, in units of 10¹² (3 significant figures). (hc = 1240 eV nm), e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
questions.solution_md: First decide which beam can act. The longest wavelength that lifts an electron across the gap is $\dfrac{1240}{1.1} \approx 1127$ nm, so the 800 nm photons (1240/800 = 1.55 eV, more than 1.1 eV) create pairs, but the 1300 nm photons (1240/1300 = 0.95 eV) do not. The 800 nm photon energy is $1.55 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 2.48 \times 10^{-19}$ J, so the pairs per second are $N = \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{0.50 \times 10^{-6}}{2.48 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.02 \times 10^{12}$, i.e. $\dfrac{2.02 \times 10^{12}}{10^{12}} = 2.02$ in units of $10^{12}$.

marking_scheme.step: Only 800 nm (1.55 eV > 1.1 eV) creates pairs; 1300 nm (0.95 eV) does not

questions.stem_md: The forbidden gap of diamond is 5.5 eV. What is the longest wavelength, in nm, that can lift an electron across the gap (3 significant figures)? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
questions.solution_md: $\lambda_{max} = \dfrac{1240}{5.5} = 225$ nm, in the ultraviolet (below 400 nm): visible light is not absorbed.

questions.stem_md: Thermal energy at room temperature is only about 0.026 eV. Explain, in terms of the forbidden gap, why silicon (gap 1.1 eV) still conducts slightly at room temperature while diamond (gap 5.5 eV) is an excellent insulator.

answer.model_answer_md: Electrons gain energies spread around the thermal value, and a few in the high-energy tail have enough to cross a gap. The number that do so falls extremely fast as the gap grows. For the 1.1 eV gap of silicon enough electrons cross to give a small conductivity; for the 5.5 eV gap of diamond practically none do, so its conduction band stays empty.

questions.solution_md: Number of electrons promoted falls extremely fast with the gap.

marking_scheme.step: A few electrons gain enough energy to cross a gap; the number falls very rapidly with the gap
Si: enough electrons cross; diamond: practically none, so it is an insulator

questions.stem_md: With the help of simple energy-band diagrams, distinguish between a conductor, an insulator and a semiconductor.

answer.model_answer_md: **Conductor:** the valence and conduction bands overlap (or the conduction band is part-filled), so there is no gap and many electrons are free at all temperatures. **Insulator:** the valence band is full and the conduction band empty, separated by a large gap (more than about 3 eV, 5.5 eV for diamond), so no electron can reach the conduction band at room temperature. **Semiconductor:** the same arrangement but with a small gap (0.7 eV for Ge, 1.1 eV for Si); it is an insulator at 0 K, but at room temperature a few electrons cross the gap, and the conductivity rises with temperature.

questions.solution_md: Overlap / large gap / small gap, with their consequences.

marking_scheme.step: Conductor: bands overlap, no gap, free electrons
Insulator: full valence band, large gap (> 3 eV), empty conduction band
Semiconductor: small gap (Ge 0.7 eV, Si 1.1 eV); some electrons cross at room temperature

questions.stem_md: A very small amount of which element, added to pure silicon, makes it an n-type semiconductor?

options.text_md: Aluminium, which has three valence electrons
Antimony, which has five valence electrons
Gallium, which has three valence electrons
Carbon, which has four valence electrons

questions.solution_md: An n-type semiconductor needs a pentavalent (group 15) donor: four of its five valence electrons fill the bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms and the fifth is almost free. Aluminium and gallium are trivalent and give p-type material — option (b).

questions.stem_md: When a battery is connected across a bar of p-type silicon, the current is carried mainly by

options.text_md: holes, as bonding electrons hop into neighbouring vacancies, so the vacancy drifts along the field
free electrons drifting through the acceptor atoms
the positive acceptor ions moving along the field
positive silicon ions moving towards the negative terminal

questions.solution_md: In p-type silicon the majority carriers are holes. A bonding electron jumps into a nearby vacancy under the field, so the vacancy appears to move in the direction of the field, like a positive charge. The ions stay fixed in the lattice — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A bar of n-type silicon is made by doping pure silicon with phosphorus. Which statement about its overall electric charge is correct?

options.text_md: It is negatively charged, because its majority carriers are electrons
It is positively charged, because phosphorus nuclei have more protons than silicon
Its charge is proportional to the number of free electrons per cubic metre
It is electrically neutral, because each free electron is balanced by the fixed positive phosphorus ion it left behind

questions.solution_md: Phosphorus atoms are neutral. When one gives up its extra electron it becomes a fixed positive ion, so for every free electron there is a fixed positive charge: the bar as a whole stays neutral — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A sample of p-type silicon is warmed by 40 K. Which statement about its carriers is most nearly correct?

options.text_md: The numbers of holes and electrons both double
The number of minority electrons rises steeply, while the number of majority holes, fixed by the acceptors, hardly changes
The number of holes falls as the number of electrons rises, keeping the total constant
Only the majority holes are affected, because the electrons are bound to their atoms

questions.solution_md: The holes of p-type silicon come mostly from the acceptors, which are already ionised at room temperature, so their number is nearly fixed. Heating breaks more bonds and creates electron–hole pairs, which adds mainly to the (very few) minority electrons, whose number grows rapidly — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A hole is a real positively charged particle, like a proton, that could be taken out of the crystal and studied on its own.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. A hole is a vacancy in a covalent bond. It behaves as a carrier of charge +e inside the crystal, but it exists only as the absence of an electron and cannot be removed from the lattice.

questions.stem_md: An indium atom has three valence electrons. When it takes the place of a silicon atom, one bond is left short of an electron, so indium is called an ___ impurity.
questions.solution_md: An **acceptor** impurity: it accepts an electron from a neighbouring bond, creating a hole, and becomes a fixed negative ion.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A bar of n-type silicon carries a net negative charge.

**Reason (R):** The majority carriers in n-type silicon are electrons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: each free electron is balanced by a fixed positive donor ion, so the bar is neutral. R is true: electrons are the majority carriers — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Match each semiconductor sample in Column A with the statement that describes it in Column B.

options.text_md: Silicon doped with antimony
Silicon doped with indium
Pure germanium at room temperature
The antimony atoms in the first sample

match_right.text_md: Electrons and holes are present in equal numbers
Donors that become fixed positive ions

questions.solution_md: Antimony (pentavalent) gives n-type: electrons are the majority carriers (1 → q); indium (trivalent) gives p-type: holes (2 → r); pure germanium is intrinsic: equal numbers (3 → p); the antimony atoms are donors that become fixed positive ions (4 → s).

questions.stem_md: Silicon has 5.0 × 10²⁸ atoms per cubic metre. If one atom in every 10⁷ is replaced by a phosphorus atom that donates one free electron, how many free electrons per cubic metre does the doping add? Give the answer in units of 10²¹ m⁻³.
questions.solution_md: Donor atoms per m³ $= 5.0 \times 10^{28} \times 10^{-7} = 5.0 \times 10^{21}$; each gives one electron, so the doping adds $5.0 \times 10^{21}$ free electrons per m³. In units of $10^{21}$ m⁻³: $n = 5.0$.

questions.stem_md: An n-type silicon bar has 5.0 × 10²¹ free electrons per cubic metre; the hole contribution can be ignored. The electron mobility is 0.135 m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. Find the resistivity of the bar, in units of 10⁻³ Ω m, to 2 significant figures. (σ = n e μ, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.solution_md: $\sigma = n e \mu = 5.0 \times 10^{21} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.135 = 108$ S m⁻¹, so $\rho = \dfrac{1}{\sigma} = 9.3 \times 10^{-3}$ Ω m. In units of $10^{-3}$ Ω m: $\rho = 9.3$.

marking_scheme.step: σ = n e μ = 108 S m⁻¹

questions.stem_md: In intrinsic silicon at 300 K the electron and hole densities are each 1.5 × 10¹⁶ per cubic metre, with mobilities 0.135 and 0.048 m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ respectively. By what factor does the conductivity rise when the silicon is doped n-type to 5.0 × 10²¹ electrons per cubic metre (electron mobility 0.135 m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, hole contribution then negligible)? Give the factor in units of 10⁵, to 2 significant figures. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.solution_md: Intrinsic: $\sigma_i = n_i e(\mu_e + \mu_h) = 1.5 \times 10^{16} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.183 = 4.39 \times 10^{-4}$ S m⁻¹. Doped: $\sigma = n e \mu_e = 5.0 \times 10^{21} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.135 = 108$ S m⁻¹. Ratio $= 2.5 \times 10^{5}$, about a quarter of a million times: one impurity atom in 10⁷ transforms the conductivity. In units of $10^{5}$: factor $= 2.5$.

marking_scheme.step: σ_i = n_i e (μe + μh) = 4.39 × 10⁻⁴ S m⁻¹
σ_doped = n e μe = 108 S m⁻¹; ratio = 2.5 × 10⁵

questions.stem_md: Describe how an n-type semiconductor is made from pure silicon, naming a suitable impurity, and state its majority and minority carriers.

answer.model_answer_md: A very small amount of a pentavalent impurity, such as phosphorus or arsenic, is added to molten silicon (doping). Each impurity atom replaces a silicon atom, uses four of its five valence electrons in bonds and gives the fifth as a free electron. The majority carriers are electrons; the minority carriers are holes.

questions.solution_md: Pentavalent donor; electrons majority, holes minority.

marking_scheme.step: Pentavalent impurity (P, As or Sb) replaces silicon atoms; its fifth electron is free

questions.stem_md: A student says: “A p-type crystal must be positively charged, because its majority carriers are holes and holes are positive.” Evaluate this statement.

answer.model_answer_md: The statement is wrong. The crystal is made of neutral atoms. When a trivalent acceptor atom captures an electron it becomes a fixed negative ion, and that creates one mobile hole. The negative ions balance the positive holes, so the p-type crystal as a whole is electrically neutral.

questions.solution_md: Holes are balanced by the fixed negative acceptor ions: neutral overall.

marking_scheme.step: Statement is wrong: the crystal is neutral
Each hole is balanced by a fixed negative acceptor ion

questions.stem_md: Explain, using the covalent-bond picture, how a p-type semiconductor is obtained from pure silicon. Say why the crystal remains neutral and name the majority carriers.

answer.model_answer_md: A trivalent impurity such as boron or indium replaces a few silicon atoms. It has only three valence electrons, so one of its four bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms is short of an electron: a **hole**. A neighbouring bonding electron can fill it, so the hole moves through the crystal. The impurity atom becomes a fixed negative ion, which balances the positive hole, so the crystal stays neutral. The majority carriers are holes.

questions.solution_md: Trivalent acceptor, one bond short, hole; neutral; holes majority.

marking_scheme.step: Trivalent impurity leaves one bond short of an electron: a hole
Acceptor becomes a fixed negative ion, balancing the hole: crystal neutral

questions.stem_md: The depletion region of an unbiased p-n junction is a thin layer that contains

options.text_md: equal numbers of free electrons and holes, recombining continuously
free electrons on the p side and free holes on the n side only
fixed negative ions on its p side and fixed positive ions on its n side, with practically no mobile carriers
a large number of mobile ions that move across the junction under the built-in field

questions.solution_md: Electrons diffuse from the n side and holes from the p side, and recombine near the junction. That uncovers fixed donor ions (positive) on the n side and fixed acceptor ions (negative) on the p side, a layer with almost no mobile carriers — option (c).

questions.stem_md: When a p-n junction diode is forward biased, the height of its potential barrier and the width of its depletion region, respectively,

options.text_md: increase and increase
decrease and decrease
decrease and increase
increase and decrease

questions.solution_md: The applied voltage opposes the built-in potential difference, so the barrier falls from V₀ to V₀ − V; a smaller barrier needs fewer uncovered ions, so the depletion region narrows — option (b).

questions.stem_md: At 25 °C a silicon diode carries a reverse current of 3 nA when the reverse voltage is 5 V. At a reverse voltage of 15 V, still well below breakdown, the current will be

options.text_md: about 9 nA, because the current is proportional to the voltage
about 3 nA, because it is carried by thermally generated minority carriers whose number does not depend on the voltage
about 1 nA, because the depletion region is wider
zero, because no current can pass in reverse bias

questions.solution_md: The reverse current is the drift of minority carriers that are generated thermally; once the field is strong enough to sweep them all across, raising the voltage does not increase their number, so the current is nearly constant (the reverse saturation current) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a circuit the p side of a germanium diode is at +1.5 V and its n side is at +1.1 V. The diode starts to conduct at about 0.3 V. Which description is correct?

options.text_md: It does not conduct, because both sides are at positive voltages
It does not conduct, because 0.4 V is less than the 0.7 V needed to overcome the barrier
It conducts, because the p side is 0.4 V above the n side, which exceeds its 0.3 V threshold
It does not conduct, because the p side is at the higher voltage

questions.solution_md: What matters is the difference of voltage between the two sides, not their values. $V_p - V_n = 1.5 - 1.1 = 0.4$ V with the p side higher, so the diode is forward biased by 0.4 V, more than the 0.3 V threshold given for germanium (0.7 V is the figure for silicon) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When a p-n junction is reverse biased, its depletion region becomes narrower and the potential barrier becomes lower.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. In reverse bias the applied voltage adds to the built-in potential difference, so the barrier rises to V₀ + V and the depletion region becomes wider.

questions.stem_md: The potential difference that builds up between the n side and the p side of an unbiased junction and stops further net diffusion of the majority carriers is called the ___ potential.
questions.solution_md: The **barrier** potential V₀ (about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The reverse current of a silicon diode hardly changes when the reverse voltage is raised from 2 V to 10 V.

**Reason (R):** Silicon has a forbidden gap of 1.1 eV.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. The reverse current is nearly constant because it is carried by thermally generated minority carriers that are all swept across at quite a low voltage; the value of the gap is not the reason — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A silicon p-n junction has a barrier potential of 0.70 V across a depletion region 0.50 μm wide. Treating the field as uniform, find the electric field in the depletion region, in units of 10⁶ V m⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $E = \dfrac{V_0}{d} = \dfrac{0.70}{0.50 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.4 \times 10^{6}$ V m⁻¹, a very strong field, directed from the n side to the p side. In units of $10^{6}$ V m⁻¹: $E = 1.4$.

questions.stem_md: A silicon diode (forward drop 0.7 V) and a 470 Ω resistor are connected in series across a 9.0 V battery, with the diode forward biased. Find the current in the circuit in mA, to 3 significant figures.
questions.solution_md: The diode drops 0.7 V, so the resistor has $9.0 - 0.7 = 8.3$ V across it: $I = \dfrac{8.3}{470} = 0.0177$ A $= 17.7$ mA.

questions.stem_md: A 12 V battery feeds two parallel branches. Branch 1 is a silicon diode D₁ (forward drop 0.7 V), forward biased, in series with 330 Ω. Branch 2 is a silicon diode D₂, reverse biased, in series with 220 Ω. Taking the reverse current as negligible, find the current drawn from the battery, in mA (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: D₂ is reverse biased and blocks, so branch 2 carries no current. In branch 1: $I = \dfrac{12 - 0.7}{330} = 0.0342$ A $= 34.2$ mA. This is the total current.

questions.stem_md: The forward current of a diode is 4.0 mA at 0.70 V and 10.0 mA at 0.73 V. Assuming the characteristic stays straight just beyond these readings, what forward voltage is needed to raise the current to 12.0 mA? Answer in volts to 3 significant figures.
questions.solution_md: First find the slope of the characteristic, the dynamic resistance: $r_d = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I} = \dfrac{0.73 - 0.70}{(10.0 - 4.0) \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{0.03}{6.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 5.0$ Ω. Raising the current from 10.0 mA to 12.0 mA adds $\Delta V = r_d \Delta I = 5.0 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3} = 0.010$ V, so the voltage needed is $0.73 + 0.010 = 0.740$ V.

questions.stem_md: A germanium diode (forward drop 0.3 V) and a silicon diode (forward drop 0.7 V) are connected in series, both forward biased, with a 400 Ω resistor and a 5.0 V battery. Find the current in mA.
questions.solution_md: The two diodes together drop $0.3 + 0.7 = 1.0$ V, leaving $5.0 - 1.0 = 4.0$ V across the resistor: $I = \dfrac{4.0}{400} = 0.010$ A $= 10.0$ mA.

marking_scheme.step: Total diode drop 1.0 V; voltage across R = 4.0 V

questions.stem_md: Explain how the potential barrier arises across a p-n junction.

answer.model_answer_md: Electrons diffuse from the n side to the p side and holes from the p side to the n side, and they recombine near the junction. This leaves positive donor ions on the n side and negative acceptor ions on the p side. These ions set up an electric field and so a potential difference V₀ across the junction, which opposes further diffusion; this is the potential barrier.

questions.solution_md: Diffusion and recombination uncover fixed ions: they create a field and a potential difference V₀.

marking_scheme.step: Diffusion and recombination leave fixed positive and negative ions near the junction
These ions give a field and potential difference V₀ that opposes further diffusion

questions.stem_md: A reverse-biased silicon diode carries only a few nanoamperes, and this hardly changes when the reverse voltage is doubled. Explain both observations.

answer.model_answer_md: In reverse bias the barrier is higher, so the majority carriers cannot cross, and the current is carried only by the very few minority carriers (thermally generated electrons on the p side and holes on the n side), which the field sweeps across the junction. Their number depends on temperature and not on the voltage, so once they are all swept across, doubling the voltage leaves the current almost unchanged.

questions.solution_md: Only minority carriers; their number is fixed by temperature.

marking_scheme.step: Current is only that of minority carriers, which are very few
Their number is set by temperature, not by the voltage, so the current is nearly constant

questions.stem_md: Describe how the depletion region and the potential barrier are formed when a p-type and an n-type semiconductor are joined, and state the direction of the built-in electric field.

answer.model_answer_md: Electrons diffuse from the n side into the p side and holes diffuse the other way, because of the difference of concentrations. They recombine near the junction, leaving a thin layer of fixed positive donor ions on the n side and fixed negative acceptor ions on the p side with no mobile carriers: the **depletion region**. The ions produce a built-in field directed from the n side to the p side and a potential barrier V₀ that stops further diffusion.

questions.solution_md: Diffusion, recombination, fixed ions, field from n to p, barrier.

marking_scheme.step: Diffusion of electrons and holes across the junction, and recombination
Layer of fixed ions with no mobile carriers: the depletion region
Built-in field from n side to p side and barrier V₀

questions.stem_md: Describe the forward and reverse V–I characteristics of a silicon p-n junction diode, stating what the knee voltage is and why the reverse current is small.

answer.model_answer_md: **Forward:** the current is negligible until the applied voltage nearly cancels the barrier; beyond the **knee voltage** (about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium) it rises very rapidly (exponentially), so the diode drops about 0.7 V while it conducts. **Reverse:** only a tiny current (nanoamperes for silicon) flows, nearly independent of the voltage, because it is carried by minority carriers, until breakdown occurs at a large reverse voltage.

questions.solution_md: Forward: knee then steep rise; reverse: tiny constant minority-carrier current.

marking_scheme.step: Forward: negligible current up to the knee voltage (about 0.7 V for Si), then a rapid rise
Reverse: very small, almost constant current, carried by minority carriers
Breakdown at a large reverse voltage; knee voltage defined as the forward voltage at which the current rises sharply

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain how the depletion region and the potential barrier are formed in a p-n junction. [2] (b) State and explain what happens to the width of the depletion region and the height of the barrier in (i) forward bias and (ii) reverse bias. [2] (c) A silicon diode (forward drop 0.7 V) is connected in series with a 330 Ω resistor across a 5.2 V battery so that it is forward biased. Find the current. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Electrons diffuse from the n side to the p side and holes the other way, and recombine near the junction. This leaves fixed positive ions on the n side and fixed negative ions on the p side with no mobile carriers: the depletion region. The ions give a field (n to p) and a barrier V₀ that stops further diffusion.

(b) (i) In forward bias the applied voltage opposes V₀: the barrier falls to V₀ − V and the depletion region narrows, so majority carriers cross easily and a large current flows. (ii) In reverse bias the applied voltage adds to V₀: the barrier rises to V₀ + V and the region widens, so only a tiny minority-carrier current flows.

(c) $I = \dfrac{5.2 - 0.7}{330} = 0.0136$ A $= 13.6$ mA.

questions.solution_md: Formation of the barrier; effect of bias; I = (E − 0.7)/R.

marking_scheme.step: Diffusion, recombination and fixed ions form the depletion region
Field and barrier V₀ stop further diffusion
Forward bias: barrier falls, region narrows, large current
Reverse bias: barrier rises, region widens, tiny current

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw the circuit with which the forward and reverse V–I characteristics of a p-n junction diode can be plotted, naming the meters and how the diode is connected in each case. [2] (b) Sketch the characteristic and mark the knee voltage and the reverse saturation current. [2] (c) In a forward-bias test the current rises from 5.0 mA to 13.0 mA as the voltage rises from 0.71 V to 0.74 V. Find the dynamic resistance of the diode. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A battery feeds a potentiometer (rheostat) used as a voltage divider; the diode is connected across the variable output through a series protective resistor. For forward bias the diode's p side is joined to the positive side, with a voltmeter across the diode and a milliammeter in series. For reverse bias the connections to the diode are reversed and a microammeter replaces the milliammeter (the voltmeter is placed across the diode).

(b) (Described in words.) Forward: the current is almost zero up to the knee at about 0.7 V (Si), then rises very steeply. Reverse: a tiny, nearly constant current (the reverse saturation current, nA to μA) until breakdown at a large reverse voltage.

(c) $r_d = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I} = \dfrac{0.74 - 0.71}{(13.0 - 5.0) \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{0.03}{8.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 3.75$ Ω.

questions.solution_md: Circuit and meters; curve with knee and I_s; r_d = ΔV/ΔI.

marking_scheme.step: Voltage-divider circuit with the diode and a series resistor
Forward: milliammeter, p side to +; reverse: connections reversed with a microammeter
Forward curve: negligible until the knee (about 0.7 V), then steep
Reverse curve: tiny, almost constant current up to breakdown

questions.stem_md: A half-wave rectifier is supplied through a transformer from a function generator set to 40 Hz. The pulsating voltage across the load has a frequency of

options.text_md: 20 Hz
40 Hz
80 Hz
zero, since the output is direct

questions.solution_md: A half-wave rectifier passes one positive half-cycle in each cycle of the input, so it gives one output pulse per input cycle: the pulses repeat at the input frequency, 40 Hz — option (b). The output is unidirectional but not steady, so its frequency is not zero.

questions.stem_md: The two-diode full-wave rectifier of a bench supply is driven from the same 40 Hz source. The frequency of the ripple in its unfiltered output is

options.text_md: 80 Hz
40 Hz
20 Hz
160 Hz

questions.solution_md: Each input cycle has two half-cycles, and the two diodes take them in turn, so the load receives two pulses per input cycle: 2 × 40 = 80 Hz — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the two-diode full-wave rectifier, the centre tap of the transformer secondary is needed to

options.text_md: reduce the peak voltage of the secondary to half its value
allow one diode to do the work of both
make the current pass through the load in both directions
provide two voltages equal in size and opposite in phase, so that each diode conducts in alternate half-cycles

questions.solution_md: With respect to the tap, the two ends of the secondary are at equal and opposite voltages. When one end is positive its diode conducts, and in the next half-cycle the other end is positive and the other diode conducts; both send current the same way through the load — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Each half of the centre-tapped secondary of a full-wave rectifier gives a peak voltage V_m. Taking the diodes as ideal, the greatest reverse voltage across the diode that is not conducting is

options.text_md: $V_m$
$\dfrac{V_m}{2}$
$\sqrt{2}\,V_m$

questions.solution_md: When D₁ conducts at the peak, its cathode is at $+V_m$ above the tap (the ideal diode has no drop). The other end of the secondary is at $-V_m$, the anode of D₂, and its cathode is joined to D₁'s cathode at $+V_m$. So D₂ has $V_m - (-V_m) = 2V_m$ across it, in reverse — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A large capacitor is connected across the load of a rectifier. It smooths the output mainly because

options.text_md: it converts the pulsating voltage into an alternating voltage of higher frequency
it raises the output voltage well above the peak of the secondary voltage
it makes the diode conduct during the whole of each cycle
it charges to the peak while the diode conducts and supplies the load as it discharges slowly when the diode stops conducting

questions.solution_md: The capacitor charges up to about the peak voltage while the diode conducts. When the input falls below that, the diode stops conducting and the capacitor keeps supplying the load, discharging only slowly through it until the next peak recharges it — option (d). Its peak is a little below the secondary peak, not above.

questions.stem_md: In a half-wave rectifier circuit the diode is accidentally connected the other way round. The output across the load will then be

options.text_md: pulses of opposite polarity, formed from the negative half-cycles of the input
zero, since the diode now blocks both half-cycles
the same as before, since the transformer supplies alternating current
an alternating voltage of the same size as the input

questions.solution_md: A diode conducts when its anode is positive with respect to its cathode. Reversed, it now conducts in the half-cycles for which the secondary terminal is negative, so the load receives the negative half-cycles as unidirectional pulses, with the opposite polarity — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The output of a rectifier that has no filter is a steady direct voltage with no variation.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The output is unidirectional but pulsating: it falls to zero (or nearly zero) between the pulses, so it needs a filter such as a capacitor to make it nearly steady.

questions.stem_md: The full-wave circuit that uses two diodes and a transformer whose secondary has a middle terminal joined to the load is called the ___ rectifier.
questions.solution_md: The **centre-tap** full-wave rectifier.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** With the same capacitor and the same load current, a full-wave rectifier gives a smaller ripple than a half-wave rectifier.

**Reason (R):** In a full-wave rectifier the capacitor has only half as long to discharge between successive peaks.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: the peaks come every 10 ms instead of every 20 ms on 50 Hz mains, so the capacitor loses half as much charge (ΔV = I t/C) before it is topped up — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The secondary of a transformer supplies 9.0 V (r.m.s.) to a half-wave rectifier that has one silicon diode, which drops 0.7 V when it conducts. Find the peak voltage across the load, in V, to 3 significant figures.
questions.solution_md: Peak secondary voltage $V_m = 9.0 \times \sqrt{2} = 12.73$ V. The diode drops 0.7 V, so the peak load voltage is $12.73 - 0.7 = 12.03$ V $\approx 12.0$ V.

questions.stem_md: A 15-0-15 V centre-tap transformer (each half of the secondary gives 15 V r.m.s.) feeds a full-wave rectifier with two silicon diodes, each dropping 0.7 V when it conducts. Find the peak voltage across the load, in V (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Only one diode conducts at a time, fed by one half of the secondary: $V_m = 15 \times \sqrt{2} = 21.21$ V. The peak load voltage is $21.21 - 0.7 = 20.51$ V $\approx 20.5$ V.

marking_scheme.step: One half of the secondary feeds one diode: V_m = 15√2 = 21.2 V

questions.stem_md: A full-wave rectifier running on 50 Hz mains has a 2200 μF capacitor across its load, which draws a steady 40 mA. Assuming that the capacitor discharges at constant current for the whole interval between successive peaks, find the peak-to-peak ripple voltage, in V (2 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: The ripple frequency is $2 \times 50 = 100$ Hz, so the capacitor discharges for $t = \dfrac{1}{100} = 0.010$ s. $\Delta V = \dfrac{I t}{C} = \dfrac{0.040 \times 0.010}{2200 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.182$ V $\approx 0.18$ V.

questions.stem_md: The primary of a transformer has 1840 turns and is connected to the 230 V mains. How many turns must the whole secondary have to give a 9-0-9 V centre-tap output (9 V r.m.s. on each half)?
questions.solution_md: The whole secondary must give $9 + 9 = 18$ V. $\dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{V_s}{V_p}$, so $N_s = 1840 \times \dfrac{18}{230} = 144$ turns, 72 on each half, with the tap at the middle.

questions.stem_md: The secondary of a transformer gives a peak voltage of 14.0 V to a half-wave rectifier that has one silicon diode. The diode conducts only while the secondary voltage exceeds 0.7 V. For what percentage of each cycle does it conduct? Give the answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.solution_md: The diode starts to conduct when $14.0 \sin\theta = 0.7$, i.e. $\sin\theta = 0.05$, $\theta_0 = 2.87^\circ$, and stops at $180^\circ - \theta_0$. It conducts for $180^\circ - 2\theta_0 = 174.3^\circ$ of each $360^\circ$ cycle: $\dfrac{174.3}{360} \times 100 = 48.4$ per cent (a little less than one half).

marking_scheme.step: Conduction angle 180° − 2θ₀ = 174.3°, which is 48.4% of the cycle

questions.stem_md: State two disadvantages of a half-wave rectifier compared with a full-wave rectifier.

answer.model_answer_md: A half-wave rectifier uses only one half of each input cycle, so half of the input power is wasted and the output is small. Its output is also a series of widely spaced pulses at the input frequency (50 Hz), so it has a large ripple that needs a much bigger filter capacitor to smooth.

questions.solution_md: One half-cycle unused; large, low-frequency ripple.

marking_scheme.step: Only one half-cycle is used: half the input is wasted, the output is small
Large low-frequency ripple, harder to filter

questions.stem_md: A half-wave and a full-wave rectifier, both run from 50 Hz mains, use the same capacitor across the same load. State which gives the smaller ripple and give the reason in terms of the time for which the capacitor discharges.

answer.model_answer_md: The full-wave rectifier gives the smaller ripple. Its output peaks every 10 ms, so the capacitor is recharged twice as often as in the half-wave circuit, where the peaks are 20 ms apart. In the shorter interval the capacitor loses only half as much charge, since ΔV = I t/C, so the ripple is half as large.

questions.solution_md: Full-wave: peaks every 10 ms, not 20 ms; ΔV = It/C is halved.

marking_scheme.step: Full-wave rectifier has the smaller ripple
Capacitor discharges for 10 ms instead of 20 ms, so ΔV = It/C is half

questions.stem_md: State the function of each of the following in a rectifier power supply: (a) the transformer, (b) the diode, (c) the filter capacitor.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The **transformer** steps the 230 V a.c. mains down to the small voltage needed (and, with a centre tap, gives two opposite-phase voltages for a full-wave circuit). (b) The **diode** conducts only when forward biased, so it lets current pass in one direction only and turns the alternating voltage into a unidirectional pulsating one. (c) The **filter capacitor** charges at the peaks and discharges slowly through the load, smoothing the pulsations into a nearly steady direct voltage.

questions.solution_md: Transformer: suitable a.c. voltage; diode: one-way conduction; capacitor: smoothing.

marking_scheme.step: Transformer: steps the mains down to the required a.c. voltage
Diode: conducts in one direction only, so rectifies
Capacitor: stores charge at the peaks and smooths the pulsating output

questions.stem_md: Draw the circuit diagram of a half-wave rectifier, and with the help of the input and output waveforms explain how it works.

answer.model_answer_md: **Circuit** (drawn in the answer): the secondary of a transformer connected in series with a diode D and a load resistor R_L. **Working:** in the half-cycle when the secondary terminal joined to the anode is positive, D is forward biased and conducts, so a current flows through R_L and the output follows the input. In the next half-cycle that terminal is negative, D is reverse biased and no current flows, so the output is zero. The output is thus a train of positive pulses, one in each input cycle, with the same frequency as the input.

questions.solution_md: Circuit; conducts in positive half-cycles; output pulses at the input frequency.

marking_scheme.step: Correct circuit: secondary, diode and load in series
Positive half-cycle: diode conducts; negative half-cycle: it blocks
Output waveform: positive pulses at the input frequency

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw the circuit diagram of a full-wave rectifier that uses two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer. [2] (b) With the help of the voltages at the two ends of the secondary and the output waveform, explain how it works. [2] (c) The input is 50 Hz mains. State the ripple frequency of the output and give a reason. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (Drawn in the answer.) The two ends A and B of the secondary go to the anodes of diodes D₁ and D₂; the cathodes are joined together to one end of the load R_L; the other end of R_L is joined to the centre tap C of the secondary.

(b) With respect to C, the voltages at A and B are equal and opposite. When A is positive, D₁ is forward biased and conducts while D₂ is reverse biased; current flows from D₁ down through R_L to C. In the next half-cycle B is positive, D₂ conducts and D₁ blocks, and the current again flows down through R_L. So both half-cycles give a current in the same direction: the output is a train of positive pulses, two for every input cycle.

(c) The ripple frequency is 100 Hz, twice the 50 Hz input, because each input cycle gives two output pulses.

questions.solution_md: Circuit; alternate conduction; 100 Hz.

marking_scheme.step: Secondary ends to the anodes of D₁ and D₂
Cathodes joined to the load, whose other end goes to the centre tap
D₁ conducts when A is positive, D₂ when B is positive; current the same way in R_L
Output: two positive pulses per input cycle (waveform)

questions.stem_md: A small power supply uses a centre-tap transformer that gives 6.0 V r.m.s. on each half of its secondary, two silicon diodes (0.7 V drop each when conducting), 50 Hz mains and a 1000 μF capacitor across the load, which draws a steady 60 mA. Find (a) the peak load voltage, [1] (b) the ripple frequency, [1] (c) the peak-to-peak ripple voltage, taking the capacitor to discharge at constant current between successive peaks, [2] (d) the ripple voltage if half-wave rectification were used instead with the same load and capacitor. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $V_m = 6.0 \times \sqrt{2} = 8.485$ V, so the peak load voltage is $8.485 - 0.7 = 7.79$ V $\approx 7.8$ V.

(b) Full-wave: $2 \times 50 = 100$ Hz.

(c) The capacitor discharges for $\dfrac{1}{100} = 0.010$ s: $\Delta V = \dfrac{I t}{C} = \dfrac{0.060 \times 0.010}{1000 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.600$ V.

(d) Half-wave: the discharge time is 0.020 s, so $\Delta V = \dfrac{0.060 \times 0.020}{1000 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.20$ V, twice as large.

questions.solution_md: V_m − 0.7; 2f; ΔV = I/(2fC) and I/(fC).

questions.stem_md: A light-emitting diode gives out light when

options.text_md: it is reverse biased, so that electrons and holes are driven apart
it is heated until a thin filament inside it glows
light falling on it creates electron–hole pairs in the depletion region
it is forward biased, so that electrons and holes recombine near the junction

questions.solution_md: In forward bias electrons from the n side and holes from the p side are pushed into the junction region, where they recombine; each recombination releases energy of about the band gap as a photon — option (d). The last option describes a photodiode or a solar cell.

questions.stem_md: A red LED and a blue LED are made from different semiconductors. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The semiconductor of the blue LED has the smaller forbidden gap, because blue light has the shorter wavelength
Both semiconductors have the same gap; the colour comes only from the tint of the plastic case
The blue LED needs the smaller forward voltage, because its photons carry less energy
The semiconductor of the blue LED has the larger forbidden gap, because each blue photon carries more energy than a red one

questions.solution_md: The photon energy is about the band gap, $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$. Blue light has the shorter wavelength, so a larger photon energy (about 2.7 eV against about 1.9 eV for red), which needs a larger gap — and a larger forward voltage — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A photodiode used as a light detector is operated in reverse bias because

options.text_md: light cannot be absorbed by a forward-biased junction
the reverse bias makes the diode emit light that it can then detect
its reverse current in the dark is tiny, so the extra current produced by light is a large fraction of the total
a forward-biased photodiode would be destroyed by the light

questions.solution_md: In the dark a reverse-biased diode passes only a very small current (nanoamperes), whereas light creates extra minority carriers that raise this current greatly in proportion. In forward bias the large forward current would hide the small change — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about a solar cell is correct?

options.text_md: It must be reverse biased by a battery in order to work
The built-in field of its p-n junction separates the electron–hole pairs made by light, so it acts as a source of emf with no external bias
It works by the recombination of electron–hole pairs and gives out light
It must be forward biased so that the junction can absorb light

questions.solution_md: Light makes electron–hole pairs near the junction; the built-in field sweeps electrons to the n side and holes to the p side, so a potential difference (about 0.5–0.7 V for silicon) appears across the cell and it drives a current through a load without any battery — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A solar cell has to be connected to a battery before it can deliver current to a load.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The built-in field of the junction separates the carriers that light creates, so the cell is itself the source of emf and needs no bias.

questions.stem_md: The energy of each photon emitted by an LED is approximately equal to the ___ of the semiconductor from which it is made.
questions.solution_md: The **band gap** (forbidden energy gap): hν ≈ Eg.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A photodiode is operated in reverse bias when it is used to detect light.

**Reason (R):** In reverse bias the current in the dark is very small, so the extra current produced by light is a large fraction of the total.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: a small dark current makes the fractional change caused by light easy to measure — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An LED gives out light when it is connected in reverse bias.

**Reason (R):** Light is emitted when electrons and holes recombine near the junction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: in reverse bias the electrons and holes are driven away from the junction and hardly recombine, so there is no light. R is true: recombination near the junction produces the photons, which needs forward bias — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Match each p-n junction device in Column A with how it is used in Column B.

options.text_md: Light-emitting diode
Photodiode
Solar cell
Zener diode

match_right.text_md: Reverse biased; its current rises with the light falling on it
Reverse biased in breakdown; holds a steady voltage
Forward biased; emits light on recombination
Unbiased; light makes it a source of emf

questions.solution_md: LED → forward bias, light from recombination (1 → r); photodiode → reverse bias, current rises with light (2 → p); solar cell → no bias, light gives an emf (3 → s); Zener diode → reverse breakdown, steady voltage (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: A red LED passes 14 mA and drops 2.0 V when it conducts. What series resistor, in Ω, is needed to run it from a 9.0 V battery?
questions.solution_md: The resistor must drop $9.0 - 2.0 = 7.0$ V at 14 mA: $R = \dfrac{7.0}{14 \times 10^{-3}} = 500$ Ω.

questions.stem_md: A blue LED emits light of wavelength 460 nm. Estimate the forbidden gap of its semiconductor, in eV, to 2 significant figures. (hc = 1240 eV nm)
questions.solution_md: $E_g \approx \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1240}{460} = 2.70$ eV $\approx 2.7$ eV.

questions.stem_md: An LED emits 3.0 mW of light of wavelength 620 nm. How many photons does it emit each second? Give the answer in units of 10¹⁵ per second (2 significant figures). (hc = 1240 eV nm; 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.solution_md: Photon energy $= \dfrac{1240}{620} = 2.00$ eV $= 3.20 \times 10^{-19}$ J. Number per second $= \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{-3}}{3.20 \times 10^{-19}} = 9.4 \times 10^{15}$ s⁻¹. In units of $10^{15}$ s⁻¹: $N = 9.4$.

questions.stem_md: A 36 W tubelight is replaced by an 18 W LED batten that gives the same light. It is used for 8 hours a day on 300 days in a year, and electricity costs ₹8 per unit (1 unit = 1 kW h). How many rupees are saved in a year?
questions.solution_md: Power saved $= 36 - 18 = 18$ W. Energy saved $= \dfrac{18 \times 8 \times 300}{1000} = 43.2$ kW h. Money saved $= 43.2 \times 8 = 346$ rupees, about ₹346.

marking_scheme.step: Energy saved = 18 W × 8 h × 300 = 43.2 kW h

questions.stem_md: A solar panel of area 1.6 m² receives sunlight of intensity 800 W m⁻² and delivers 224 W of electrical power. Find its efficiency as a percentage.
questions.solution_md: Power received $= 800 \times 1.6 = 1280$ W. Efficiency $= \dfrac{224}{1280} \times 100 = 17.5\%$.

questions.stem_md: A silicon photodiode in reverse bias receives 1.0 μW of light of wavelength 850 nm. Each photon creates one electron–hole pair, and a pair is collected as current with probability 0.70. Find the photocurrent, in μA, to 2 significant figures. (hc = 1240 eV nm; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.solution_md: Photon energy $= \dfrac{1240}{850} = 1.459$ eV $= 2.33 \times 10^{-19}$ J. Photons per second $= \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-6}}{2.33 \times 10^{-19}} = 4.28 \times 10^{12}$ s⁻¹. Carriers collected per second $= 0.70 \times 4.28 \times 10^{12} = 3.00 \times 10^{12}$, so $I = 3.00 \times 10^{12} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 4.8 \times 10^{-7}$ A $= 0.48$ μA.

marking_scheme.step: Photon energy 1240/850 = 1.46 eV; photons per second = 4.3 × 10¹²

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why replacing filament lamps by LED lamps saves energy and reduces pollution.

answer.model_answer_md: An LED changes a much larger fraction of the electrical energy into light, whereas a filament lamp wastes most of it as heat, so an LED needs far less power for the same light, and it also lasts many times longer. The smaller demand for electricity means less coal and oil burnt in power stations, and so less carbon dioxide and other pollutants released.

questions.solution_md: Higher efficiency (little heat), longer life; less fuel burnt, less pollution.

marking_scheme.step: An LED turns far more of the electrical energy into light (little heat) and lasts longer: less power for the same light
Less electricity is needed, so less fuel is burnt and less carbon dioxide is released

questions.stem_md: A silicon photodiode (forbidden gap 1.1 eV) gives a strong signal for light of wavelength 850 nm but none at all for light of wavelength 1300 nm, however intense. Use the photon energies to explain this.

answer.model_answer_md: The photon energy is $\dfrac{1240}{\lambda}$ eV. At 850 nm it is 1.46 eV, which is more than 1.1 eV, so each photon can lift an electron across the gap and make an electron–hole pair. At 1300 nm it is 0.954 eV, less than the gap, so no photon can make a pair, and a brighter beam only supplies more photons that are all too weak.

questions.solution_md: hν must exceed Eg: 1.46 eV works, 0.95 eV does not.

marking_scheme.step: 850 nm: photon energy 1.46 eV > 1.1 eV, so pairs are made
1300 nm: 0.95 eV < 1.1 eV, no pairs however many photons

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an LED, a photodiode and a solar cell in terms of (i) the bias used and (ii) the part played by light.

answer.model_answer_md: **LED:** forward biased; it gives out light, produced when electrons and holes recombine near the junction. **Photodiode:** reverse biased; it takes in light, which creates electron–hole pairs in the depletion region and so raises the reverse current in proportion to the intensity. **Solar cell:** no bias at all; it takes in light, and the junction field separates the pairs it creates, so the cell is itself a source of emf.

questions.solution_md: LED: forward, emits; photodiode: reverse, detects; solar cell: unbiased, generates.

marking_scheme.step: LED: forward bias; light is emitted by recombination
Photodiode: reverse bias; light creates pairs and raises the reverse current
Solar cell: no bias; light creates pairs that the junction field separates, giving an emf

questions.stem_md: Explain the working of a solar cell. Why is no battery needed, and why is the junction made with a large area?

answer.model_answer_md: A solar cell is a p-n junction (a thin p layer on an n layer). Photons with hν > Eg that reach the depletion region and its neighbourhood create electron–hole pairs. The built-in field sweeps the electrons to the n side and the holes to the p side, so a potential difference appears across the cell (about 0.5 V to 0.7 V for silicon) and current flows through an external load from p to n. The junction field itself separates the charges, so no battery is needed. A large area intercepts more light and so gives a larger current.

questions.solution_md: Pairs created by light; junction field separates them; emf; large area for more current.

marking_scheme.step: Photons with hν > Eg create electron–hole pairs near the junction
The built-in field separates them: electrons to n, holes to p; emf across the cell, so no battery is needed
Large area collects more light, giving a larger current

questions.stem_md: (a) With the help of a band picture, explain how an LED gives out light and in what kind of bias it is used. [2] (b) An LED is made from a semiconductor of band gap 2.1 eV. Find the wavelength of the light it emits and say whether it is visible. (hc = 1240 eV nm) [2] (c) Give one advantage of an LED lamp over a filament lamp. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The LED is a p-n junction used in forward bias. Electrons from the n side and holes from the p side are pushed into the junction region; there an electron falls from the conduction band into a hole in the valence band (recombination) and the energy of about the band gap leaves as a photon.

(b) $\lambda \approx \dfrac{hc}{E_g} = \dfrac{1240}{2.1} = 590$ nm, in the visible range (yellow-orange).

(c) An LED lamp gives the same light for much less electrical power, and it lasts much longer.

questions.solution_md: Forward bias, recombination; λ = hc/Eg; advantage.

marking_scheme.step: Forward-biased junction: electrons and holes recombine
Energy ≈ Eg released as a photon
Advantage: much lower power for the same light, or a much longer life

questions.stem_md: A Zener diode is used as a voltage regulator by connecting it

options.text_md: in reverse bias, in parallel with the load, with a resistor in series with the supply
in forward bias, in series with the load
in reverse bias, in series with the load, with no other resistor
in forward bias, in parallel with the load, with no series resistor

questions.solution_md: The Zener works in its reverse breakdown region, so it is connected in reverse bias across the load (parallel). The series resistor takes the excess voltage and limits the current so that the diode is not damaged — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the breakdown region of a Zener diode, when the current through it changes over a wide range, the voltage across it

options.text_md: changes in proportion to the current
falls to zero
stays almost constant, at the Zener voltage
rises steadily above the Zener voltage

questions.solution_md: The reverse characteristic is almost vertical at the Zener voltage V_Z: large changes of current produce only tiny changes of voltage, which is why the diode can hold a voltage steady — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a Zener regulator the load resistance is decreased, with the input voltage unchanged and the Zener diode still in breakdown. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The load current rises and the Zener current falls by the same amount, while the output voltage stays at the Zener voltage
The load current rises and the Zener current rises by the same amount
The current in the series resistor increases and the output voltage falls
The output voltage rises because the load draws more current

questions.solution_md: With the output fixed at V_Z, the current in the series resistor, (V_in − V_Z)/R_s, is constant. The load current V_Z/R_L rises as R_L falls, so the Zener current, which is the difference, falls by the same amount — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A 6.0 V Zener diode is fed from a 10 V supply through a 220 Ω series resistor, and a load is connected across the diode. The load resistance is made smaller and smaller, until the load would need more current than the series resistor can supply at 6.0 V. Then

options.text_md: the Zener current increases to make up the difference and the output stays at 6.0 V
the Zener diode stops conducting and the output voltage falls below 6.0 V
the output voltage rises above 6.0 V
the output stays at 6.0 V, because a Zener diode holds the voltage constant whatever the load

questions.solution_md: At 6.0 V the series resistor supplies at most $\dfrac{10 - 6.0}{220} = 18.2 \times 10^{-3}$ A, so the load can take at most that (this is for $R_L \approx 330$ Ω). For a smaller $R_L$ the Zener current would have to be negative; instead it drops to zero, the diode leaves breakdown and the output is just the potential divider voltage $10 \times \dfrac{R_L}{220 + R_L}$, below 6.0 V — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In forward bias a Zener diode behaves much like an ordinary silicon diode.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Its forward characteristic is like that of an ordinary junction diode, with a knee at about 0.7 V; its special behaviour is in reverse breakdown.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A Zener diode in its reverse breakdown region can hold the voltage across a load nearly constant.

**Reason (R):** In breakdown the current through a Zener diode stays almost constant while the voltage across it changes greatly.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: it is the other way about. In breakdown the voltage stays almost constant while the current changes over a wide range — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A 6.8 V Zener diode is to regulate the voltage across a load that draws up to 20 mA from a 12 V supply, and the Zener diode must carry at least 5.0 mA at all times. Find the largest series resistance, in Ω, that can be used.
questions.solution_md: The series resistor carries $I = I_L + I_Z = 20 + 5.0 = 25$ mA at the least, with $12 - 6.8 = 5.2$ V across it: $R_s = \dfrac{5.2}{25 \times 10^{-3}} = 208$ Ω. A larger resistance would pass too little current when the load is at its maximum.

marking_scheme.step: I = I_L + I_Z = 25 mA and V across R_s = 5.2 V

questions.stem_md: In a Zener regulator the input is 15 V, the series resistor is 470 Ω, the Zener voltage is 9.1 V and the load resistance is 1.0 kΩ. Find the current through the Zener diode, in mA (2 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: The output is held at 9.1 V, so the resistor has $15 - 9.1 = 5.9$ V across it: $I = \dfrac{5.9}{470} = 12.55 \times 10^{-3}$ A. Load current $I_L = \dfrac{9.1}{1000} = 9.1 \times 10^{-3}$ A. Zener current $I_Z = I - I_L = 12.55 - 9.1 \approx 3.5$ mA.

questions.stem_md: A 5.1 V Zener diode, a 150 Ω series resistor and a fixed 510 Ω load form a regulator. The current through the Zener diode must stay between 2.0 mA and 30 mA. Find the largest input voltage that can be used, in V (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Load current $= \dfrac{5.1}{510} = 10 \times 10^{-3}$ A. At the largest input the Zener carries 30 mA, so the series resistor carries $10 + 30 = 40$ mA. $V_{in} = V_Z + I R_s = 5.1 + 0.040 \times 150 = 11.1$ V. (The smallest input, for 2.0 mA in the Zener, is 6.90 V.)

marking_scheme.step: I_L = 5.1/510 = 10 mA; resistor current 40 mA at the maximum

questions.stem_md: A regulator has a 10 V input, a 220 Ω series resistor and a 6.0 V Zener diode that must carry at least 2.0 mA to stay in breakdown. Find the smallest load resistance, in Ω, for which the output stays at 6.0 V (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Current in the series resistor $= \dfrac{10 - 6.0}{220} = 18.18 \times 10^{-3}$ A. The most the load can take is $18.18 - 2.0 = 16.18$ mA, so $R_{L,min} = \dfrac{6.0}{0.01618} = 371$ Ω.

questions.stem_md: A Zener regulator has a 180 Ω series resistor. The input rises from 12.0 V to 13.5 V, with the load fixed and the Zener diode in breakdown throughout. By how much does the Zener current increase, in mA (2 significant figures)?
questions.solution_md: The output is held constant, so the whole 1.5 V rise appears across the series resistor and the load current does not change. $\Delta I_Z = \Delta I = \dfrac{1.5}{180} = 8.33 \times 10^{-3}$ A; to 2 significant figures $\Delta I_Z = 8.3$ mA.

marking_scheme.step: ΔI = 1.5/180 = 8.3 mA, all of it passing through the Zener

questions.stem_md: Describe the reverse V–I characteristic of a Zener diode and show on it the Zener voltage.

answer.model_answer_md: In reverse bias the current is very small until the reverse voltage reaches a value V_Z, the Zener voltage. At V_Z the current suddenly rises very steeply, and then changes through a wide range with the voltage across the diode staying almost equal to V_Z (the curve is nearly vertical). In forward bias it behaves like an ordinary diode.

questions.solution_md: Tiny current up to V_Z, then a nearly vertical rise.

marking_scheme.step: Reverse current is negligible up to the Zener (breakdown) voltage V_Z
At V_Z the current rises steeply, the voltage staying almost constant at V_Z

questions.stem_md: Draw the circuit of a Zener diode voltage regulator and explain how it keeps the output voltage constant when the input voltage rises.

answer.model_answer_md: **Circuit** (drawn in the answer): the supply feeds a series resistor R_s; the Zener diode, connected in reverse (cathode to the positive side), and the load R_L are in parallel across the output. **Action:** the Zener is in breakdown, so its voltage, and so the output, is fixed at V_Z. If the input rises, the current in R_s increases and the extra current flows through the Zener, whose voltage hardly changes; the extra voltage drops across R_s. The output therefore stays at V_Z.

questions.solution_md: Circuit; extra current through the Zener; extra voltage across R_s.

marking_scheme.step: Circuit: R_s in series, reverse-biased Zener in parallel with the load
Zener in breakdown fixes the output at V_Z
Input rise: extra current through the Zener, extra voltage across R_s

questions.stem_md: A Zener regulator keeps 6.0 V across its load, and the series resistor carries a steady 30 mA. Find the load current and the Zener current when the load resistance is (i) 600 Ω and (ii) 400 Ω, and explain the change.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $I_L = \dfrac{6.0}{600} = 10.0 \times 10^{-3}$ A, so $I_Z = 30 - 10.0 = 20.0$ mA. (ii) $I_L = \dfrac{6.0}{400} = 15.0 \times 10^{-3}$ A, so $I_Z = 30 - 15.0 = 15.0$ mA. The output stays at 6.0 V, so the current in the series resistor stays 30 mA; when the load takes more, the Zener takes correspondingly less.

questions.solution_md: I_L = V_Z/R_L; I_Z = I − I_L.

marking_scheme.step: Total current fixed at 30 mA: the Zener current falls as the load current rises

questions.stem_md: A regulator uses a 9.1 V Zener diode, a 220 Ω series resistor and a fixed 910 Ω load. The Zener current must lie between 3.0 mA and 40 mA. Find (i) the load current, (ii) the smallest and (iii) the largest input voltage that can be used.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $I_L = \dfrac{9.1}{910} = 10.0 \times 10^{-3}$ A. (ii) Smallest input: the Zener carries 3.0 mA, so the series resistor carries $10 + 3.0 = 13$ mA and $V_{in} = 9.1 + 0.013 \times 220 = 11.96$ V $\approx 12.0$ V. (iii) Largest input: the Zener carries 40 mA, so the resistor carries 50 mA and $V_{in} = 9.1 + 0.050 \times 220 = 20.1$ V.

questions.solution_md: V_in = V_Z + (I_L + I_Z)R_s at the two limits.

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw the circuit of a voltage regulator using a Zener diode. [1] (b) Explain how it keeps the output voltage constant when the input voltage rises. [2] (c) A 6.0 V Zener diode regulates the supply to a 600 Ω load from a 12 V source, and is to carry 10 mA. Find the series resistance needed and the power dissipated in the Zener diode. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (Drawn in the answer.) A series resistor R_s joins the 12 V source to the output; the Zener diode, connected in reverse (cathode towards the positive terminal), is in parallel with the load R_L.

(b) The Zener diode works in its reverse breakdown region, where its voltage stays at V_Z for a wide range of currents. If the input voltage rises, the current in R_s rises, and the whole increase flows through the Zener diode while the voltage across it, and so across the load, stays at V_Z; the extra voltage is dropped across R_s.

(c) Load current $I_L = \dfrac{6.0}{600} = 10.0 \times 10^{-3}$ A. Current in R_s $= 10 + 10 = 20.0$ mA. $R_s = \dfrac{12 - 6.0}{0.0200} = 300$ Ω. Power in the Zener $= V_Z I_Z = 6.0 \times 10 \times 10^{-3} = 0.0600$ W $= 60.0$ mW.

questions.solution_md: Circuit; breakdown and extra current; R_s = (V_in − V_Z)/(I_L + I_Z); P = V_Z I_Z.

marking_scheme.step: Series resistor with a reverse-biased Zener across the load
Zener in breakdown holds the voltage at V_Z over a wide current range
Input rise: extra current through the Zener and extra voltage across R_s
